cards.front: At which OSI layer does AWS WAF work, and what does that let it inspect?
cards.back: **Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS).** It can read the URI, query string, headers, cookies, body, source IP and country of each web request, so it can stop attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting.

cards.front: Name five resource types you can attach an AWS WAF web ACL to.
cards.back: **CloudFront** distributions, **Application Load Balancers**, **API Gateway REST APIs**, **AppSync GraphQL APIs** and **Cognito user pools** (also App Runner, Verified Access, Amplify and Bedrock AgentCore Gateway).
cards.updated: App Runner, Verified Access, Amplify and Bedrock AgentCore Gateway were added after the slides.

cards.front: Can you attach AWS WAF to a Network Load Balancer?
cards.back: **No.** An NLB works at layer 4 and WAF needs an HTTP-terminating resource. For static IPs plus WAF, put **Global Accelerator** in front of an **ALB** that carries the web ACL.

cards.front: In which Region must you create a WAF web ACL for a CloudFront distribution? And for an ALB?
cards.back: CloudFront: **US East (N. Virginia), us-east-1** (the global "CloudFront" scope). ALB and other Regional resources: the **same Region as the resource**.

cards.front: How many IP addresses (CIDR ranges) can one WAF IP set hold, and what do you do if you need more?
cards.back: Up to **10,000** CIDR ranges per IP set. For more, create additional IP sets and reference them from additional rules.

cards.front: What does a WAF rate-based rule do, and what windows and minimum limit can you choose?
cards.back: It counts requests per aggregation key (by default each source IP) and applies an action, usually Block, once a key exceeds the limit. Windows: **1, 2, 5 (default) or 10 minutes**; lowest limit **10**.
cards.updated: Older material shows only a 5-minute window and a minimum of 100.

cards.front: What is a WAF rule group?
cards.back: A **reusable set of rules** you can add to one or many web ACLs: your own, **AWS Managed Rules** (core rule set, SQL database, IP reputation and more) or AWS Marketplace groups.

cards.front: Which WAF rule action lets you test a new rule against live traffic without affecting it?
cards.back: **Count.** It records matches (metrics, sampled requests, logs) and continues evaluating the remaining rules, so nothing is blocked.

cards.front: What does AWS Shield Standard cost and what does it protect against?
cards.back: It is **free and automatic** for every AWS customer. It defends against common **layer 3/4** DDoS attacks such as **SYN floods and UDP reflection**, with the strongest coverage for CloudFront, Route 53 and Global Accelerator.

cards.front: What does Shield Advanced cost?
cards.back: **USD 3,000 per month** with a **1-year commitment**, billed once per organization's payer account, plus data transfer out fees for protected resources.

cards.front: List four things Shield Advanced adds on top of Shield Standard.
cards.back: 24/7 **Shield Response Team (SRT)**; **cost protection** against DDoS-driven scaling charges; detailed **attack visibility** and alarms; **layer 7 DDoS protection** (now the included WAF Anti-DDoS managed rule group). WAF fees and Firewall Manager policies for protected resources are also included.

cards.front: Which resource types can Shield Advanced protect?
cards.back: **CloudFront** distributions, **Route 53** hosted zones, **Global Accelerator** standard accelerators, **ALB** and **CLB**, and **Elastic IP addresses** (which covers EC2 instances and NLBs attached to them).

cards.front: What replaced Shield Advanced's layer 7 automatic mitigation as the default for HTTP floods in 2026?
cards.back: The AWS WAF **Anti-DDoS managed rule group** (`AWSManagedRulesAntiDDoSRuleSet`), default since 26 March 2026. It reacts within seconds and is included for Shield Advanced subscribers; existing customers can keep the older automatic mitigation.
cards.updated: Change made in March 2026, after the slides.

cards.front: What are the prerequisites for AWS Firewall Manager?
cards.back: An organization in **AWS Organizations** (all features), a designated Firewall Manager **administrator account**, and **AWS Config** enabled in the accounts and Regions you want to protect.

cards.front: Which policy types can Firewall Manager apply across an organization?
cards.back: **AWS WAF**, **Shield Advanced**, **VPC security groups**, **VPC network ACLs**, **AWS Network Firewall**, **Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall** and **third-party firewalls** (Palo Alto Cloud NGFW, Fortigate CNF).
cards.updated: Network ACL and third-party firewall policies are newer than the slides.

cards.front: WAF alone or Firewall Manager with WAF: how do you choose?
cards.back: **WAF alone** for granular rules on your own resources. **Firewall Manager + WAF** when the same rules must cover many accounts and be applied automatically to new accounts and resources.

cards.front: Which AWS services make up the edge layer of the DDoS best practices (BP1, BP3)?
cards.back: **CloudFront** and **Global Accelerator** (BP1) and **Route 53** (BP3). They absorb and filter floods at edge locations before traffic reaches your Region; Global Accelerator suits non-HTTP backends.

cards.front: How do you reduce the attack surface of an application in AWS?
cards.back: Hide backends (EC2, Lambda) behind **CloudFront, API Gateway or ELB**; keep instances in private subnets; restrict **security groups and NACLs** to expected traffic; protect APIs with throttling, authentication and WAF.

cards.front: Which three data sources does GuardDuty analyze as soon as you enable it?
cards.back: **CloudTrail management events**, **VPC Flow Logs** and **Route 53 Resolver DNS query logs**. It reads its own copy, so you do not need to enable these logs yourself.

cards.front: Name four optional GuardDuty protection plans.
cards.back: Any four of: **S3 Protection**, **EKS Protection**, **Runtime Monitoring**, **Malware Protection** (EC2, S3, AWS Backup), **RDS Protection**, **Lambda Protection**, **AI Protection**.
cards.updated: Runtime Monitoring, Malware Protection for S3 and AWS Backup, and AI Protection are newer than the slides.

cards.front: How do you get an email or trigger a fix automatically when GuardDuty raises a finding?
cards.back: Create an **EventBridge rule** matching `source: aws.guardduty` (detail-type `GuardDuty Finding`) and target an **SNS topic** for email or a **Lambda function** for remediation.

cards.front: How long is the GuardDuty free trial?
cards.back: **30 days** per Region, starting the first time you enable GuardDuty there. Protection plans switched on at that moment (all except Runtime Monitoring) are included.

cards.front: How long does GuardDuty keep findings?
cards.back: **90 days.** To keep them longer, configure findings export to an **S3 bucket** (or forward the EventBridge events to your own storage).

cards.front: Which three resource types does Amazon Inspector scan for vulnerabilities?
cards.back: **EC2 instances** (packages and network reachability), **container images in Amazon ECR** (on push and continuously) and **Lambda functions** (dependencies and, optionally, code).

cards.front: How does Inspector collect the software inventory of an EC2 instance?
cards.back: **Agent-based** through the **SSM Agent** (the instance must be an SSM managed instance), or **agentless** from **EBS snapshots** for instances without the agent (hybrid scanning).
cards.updated: Agentless EBS-snapshot scanning is newer than the slides.

cards.front: What is the Amazon Inspector risk score?
cards.back: A per-finding score in CVSS format: the CVE's base score **adjusted to your environment**, for example lowered when a network-exploitable flaw sits on an instance with no network path from outside.

cards.front: What does Amazon Macie do?
cards.back: It uses **machine learning and pattern matching** to find **sensitive data (PII, financial data, credentials) in Amazon S3**, and raises policy findings when a bucket's security weakens, such as becoming public.

cards.front: Macie: automated sensitive data discovery versus a sensitive data discovery job?
cards.back: **Automated discovery** samples objects across all buckets continuously for broad visibility. A **job** analyzes buckets you choose, once or on a schedule, with your own scope and sampling depth.

cards.front: GuardDuty, Inspector or Macie: which one for (a) crypto-mining on EC2, (b) a CVE in an ECR image, (c) credit card numbers in S3?
cards.back: (a) **GuardDuty** (behaviour in logs, it has crypto-mining finding types), (b) **Inspector** (software vulnerabilities), (c) **Macie** (sensitive data in S3).

cards.front: What is AWS Security Hub CSPM?
cards.back: The posture-management service (formerly just "Security Hub") that runs best-practice checks and **aggregates findings** from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie and partners in one place.
cards.updated: Renamed Security Hub CSPM after the slides.
